job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Femi Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the second semester of a master's in software systems at Marlow Park University. Mornings I'm in a lab writing a scheduler for a thesis project, and afternoons I do lectures or tutor first-years in programming for pocket money. I finished my bachelor's top of the class, with internships at a freight software firm and in the IT team of the city council. My dad drives buses and I still eat at his flat on Sundays. I write all my code by hand, because I don't trust the AI tools to be right and I don't like how they were trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's what I always thought. Fine, it saves a few minutes on boilerplate, but the people who sold it as magic were selling something. At the lab we'd just keep doing real engineering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's a relief, because I never wanted to rely on those tools. Still, I'm doing a master's partly because the junior job market is thin, and that doesn't change. I have about two months of savings and a student loan sitting at 14,000.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, apply to around 30 firms this spring, and keep tutoring on Tuesdays and Thursdays. My dad says the council's IT team might open a post next year, so I'd keep in touch with my old internship supervisor, Mrs Adeyemi.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, but with a tight feeling underneath. The loan and the rent worry me more than any machine does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the junior market is thin even without a big AI shift. What makes it thin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Firms hire fewer juniors when money is tight. My cohort had 60 people and I know maybe 15 who have real offers. I think firms blame cost, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first if the job search drags on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym and the streaming subscription go in a day. After that my share of the flat rent, 380 a month, and my dad would quietly cover it. I hate that thought.

say: It's mostly **hype**, and engineers should say so plainly.
Companies should stop using AI as an excuse for **cutting** junior hiring.
think: I'm relieved I never leaned on **AI tools** and so lost no skills.
The thin junior market and my **14,000 loan** are my real worry.
do: Finish the master's and apply to about **30 firms** this spring.
Keep **tutoring** twice a week to cover rent.
Stay in touch with my old council IT **supervisor**.
feel: Steady on the surface, with a tight feeling about **money** underneath.
S0.quote: The loan and the rent worry me more than any machine does.
fieldNote: Femi is relieved but not calm: his money pressure exists with or without **AI**.
He never uses AI tools, so this card confirms his view rather than testing it.

steps.text: Keep tutoring first-years in programming on Tuesdays and Thursdays
Send 30 job applications to software firms this spring
Finish the thesis scheduler and carry on at the same pace

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's where I get angry. If AI does coding, checking and planning, junior engineers like me are exactly who firms stop hiring, and they'll call it progress. Someone has to say that out loud, preferably a union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my plan of writing everything by hand turns into a handicap. A manager with a budget will pick the person who produces twice as fast with a tool. I'm good, but I'm slow to pick up new tools and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd join a union for tech workers, because my dad's union got him a decent deal. I'd also force myself to use one AI tool for a month on a side project, just to see its limits. And I'd widen my search to the council, the hospital IT team and the rail company, where people can't be swapped for software overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry and a bit ashamed. Angry at firms, ashamed that I'm digging in while the world moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd test one tool for a month. What would make you actually do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fear, honestly. If two of my friends get offers because they're fast with the tools and I don't, I'll do it that week. I'd rather do it before that happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister, who starts a computing degree next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my younger sister to do the degree but learn the tools from day one, and to join a union as soon as she has a job. I'd be a hypocrite saying it, but it's true.

say: AI taking junior tasks is a **political** problem, not a technical one.
Tech workers need a **union** and rules on hiring.
think: My **hand-written** habits could become a handicap against faster colleagues.
I'm **slow** to adopt tools and I know it.
do: Join a tech workers' **union** within the first few months.
Test one **AI tool** for a month on a side project.
Apply to the council, hospital and rail **IT teams**.
feel: **Angry** at firms and a bit ashamed of digging in.
S1.quote: I'd tell my younger sister to do the degree but learn the tools from day one, and to join a union as soon as she has a job.
fieldNote: Femi's politics shape how he blames **firms**, but he also admits his own **resistance** is a risk.
Fear is his trigger for change, not curiosity.

steps.text: Join a union for tech workers and go to its first meeting
Try one AI coding tool for a month on a side project
Apply to the council, the hospital and the rail company IT teams

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. I'd be quiet at first, then loud. I'd say governments must slow down, set rules and protect workers, because families haven't had time to think. The online chat would explode and my posts would too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the entry-level coding job I trained for is gone before I even graduate from the master's. My top marks and two internships turn into nothing, because a firm would just buy the tool. And my dad, who thinks I'm set for life, doesn't see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the second year of the master's if it isn't going to lead anywhere, which is a big thing for me. I'd go to the union and the local party office and push for a public jobs guarantee. I'd also look for work in places where I physically show up, like the bus depot, because robots take about three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel sick, honestly. I did the right thing for years and then somebody changed the rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd consider leaving the master's. What would that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan stays whether I finish or not, and a degree sitting half done is awkward to explain. But paying another 8,000 for something that might not matter hurts more. I'd talk to my thesis supervisor first, Dr Haile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say Dad (his father), please don't tell me it'll sort itself out. Then I'd ask him how the bus drivers' union would handle self-driving buses, because that's coming three years after the AI.

say: Governments must **slow down**, set rules and protect workers right now.
Two years gives families and schools no time to **prepare**.
think: The **entry-level** coding job I trained for may vanish before I finish.
My top marks might count for **nothing**.
do: Talk to my supervisor about **stopping** the master's.
Push the union and local party for a **jobs guarantee**.
Look for work in **physical** places like the bus depot.
feel: **Sick**, like the rules changed after I played by them.
S2.quote: I did the right thing for years and then somebody changed the rules.
fieldNote: Femi expects the **junior** job he trained for to vanish and says it is keeping him up at night.
His first response is **political** and only second personal, which matches his union background.

steps.text: Ask Dr Haile whether to stop the master's after this semester
Push the union and local party office for a public jobs guarantee
Join the tech workers' union and go to every meeting
Apply for IT support work at the bus depot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to fight about it properly. I'd say we need a plan: retraining funded by the firms that profit, and shorter working weeks. I'd organise with other graduates, because on our own we're weak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be anxious but not hopeless. By 2031 I'd be 29 and maybe three years into a job, so I'd be an employee with a union card and some savings, not a fresh graduate with nothing. That's a better position than 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first decent job I'm offered, even if the pay is average, and stay long enough to build a track record. I'd save a quarter of each salary into a safe account, and finally learn the AI tools properly, because by then refusing is silly. If I can, I'd also move into the safety or testing side of software, where a human signature still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense but not frozen. I can picture a path, and that helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me get one real job on my record and a cushion in the bank, and that's the difference between a bad week and a bad decade. In two years I'd be starting from zero with the loan still on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tools properly. Why then and not now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because now I can still tell myself it's optional. A deadline that is real makes it a decision. It's not my best quality, but it's the truth.

say: We need a **plan**: retraining paid for by the firms that profit from it.
Graduates should **organise** together early, because alone we're weak.
think: With five years I could be an employee with **savings** instead of a graduate with nothing.
do: Take the first decent **job** and build a record.
Save **a quarter** of each salary in a safe account.
Learn the **AI tools** properly once the date is real.
feel: **Tense** but not frozen, because there's a path to picture.
S3.quote: Five years lets me get one real job on my record and a cushion in the bank, and that's the difference between a bad week and a bad decade.
fieldNote: Femi's mood eases with more time because he can see himself employed and **saving**.
He finally says he would use **AI tools** once refusing becomes silly.

steps.text: Accept the first decent software job and stay a couple of years
Move a quarter of every salary into a safe savings account
Take an evening course on using AI coding tools properly
Organise a monthly meet-up of graduates in the union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time, so I'd be calmer in public. I'd say the real fight is making sure the gains are shared, and that means voting and organising, not panicking. The tech industry has a tradition of promising things and not delivering, so I'd also say we should wait to see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it gives me real room. By 2036 I'd be 34, possibly with a family, and I could have paid off the loan and grown into something like a team lead. I'd still worry about the 3 years after the AI when robots catch up, but that's for my sister's generation as much as mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the master's properly, work for a few years, and pay off the loan first. I'd probably go into a field with a human in the loop, such as public sector IT or systems safety. And I'd stay active in the union, because I think the argument will be settled in the next few elections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. It's the first one where I can plan a normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years make your resistance to the tools matter less or more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less, because I have time to learn them at my own speed. But I'd still avoid anything that scrapes people's work without asking, and I'd want clear rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything in your private plan you wouldn't say online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I want a family and a flat before 32. I don't say that online, because it sounds like I've given up on the fight.

say: The real fight is sharing the **gains**, through votes and organising.
The industry has a habit of **over-promising**, so I'd wait and see.
think: Ten years gives me **room** to pay off the loan and grow.
The robot years worry me more for my **sister's** generation.
do: Finish the master's, work, and clear the **14,000 loan** first.
Aim for public sector or **safety** IT work.
Stay active in the **union** through the next elections.
feel: **Fairly calm**, because I can plan a normal life.
S4.quote: I want a family and a flat before 32. I don't say that online, because it sounds like I've given up on the fight.
fieldNote: Femi is calmest here: a decade lets him picture **loan** paid, a family and union work.
His public and private lines differ most on **family** plans.

steps.text: Pay off the 14,000 student loan before taking on a flat
Aim to rent a flat with a partner by age 32
Vote and volunteer in the next two elections for worker protections
Look for public sector or safety-focused IT roles

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Two years gives me no time to get a real job on my record or a cushion in the bank. What would help is a public jobs guarantee, wage support while people retrain, and firms being told they can't drop junior hiring overnight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm more frightened of my own stubbornness than of the machines, and I don't say that to my union friends. I'd like someone to tell me that learning the tools doesn't make me a traitor.

headlineQuote: I'm more frightened of my own stubbornness than of the machines, and I don't say that to my union friends.
portrait: Femi is a 24-year-old **computer science** graduate doing a master's, with a 14,000 student loan.
He writes code by hand, never uses **AI tools**, and favours unions and regulation, like his bus-driver dad.
He blames firms for cutting **junior** jobs, but privately fears his own slowness to adapt.
His mood climbs from uneasy to **alarmed** at two years, then back to calm at ten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves no time for a record or a cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A public **jobs guarantee**, wage support during retraining and limits on dropping junior hiring.
Permission to learn the tools without feeling like a **traitor**.
